title: The ER Model and Normalisation: Designing Good Schemas

questions.question: In an ER diagram, students take many courses and each course holds many students. How is this M:N relationship mapped to relational tables?
options: A foreign key on the student table
A foreign key on the course table
A junction table whose key is the pair of both entity keys
The two tables are merged into one
questions.rationale: The relational model has no native M:N construct, so the relationship becomes its own table — ENROLMENT(student_id, course_id, grade) — holding both keys as a composite primary key.

questions.question: A STUDENT row stores a phone column containing "98110, 99201". Which normal form does this violate?
questions.rationale: First normal form requires atomic values with no repeating groups; two phones in one cell force string surgery for queries, so each phone moves to its own row in a separate table.

questions.question: In ENROLMENT_REPORT keyed by (student_id, course_id), the name column depends on student_id alone. This violates:
options: 2NF, because name depends on part of the composite key
BCNF, because name is a determinant
questions.rationale: Second normal form forbids partial dependencies — non-key attributes determined by only part of a composite key — which is exactly the sid-to-name situation; the fix is splitting out STUDENT.

questions.question: student_id → hostel_id and hostel_id → hostel_name together give student_id → hostel_name. What is this pattern called, and which normal form forbids it among non-key attributes?
questions.rationale: When a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute (hostel_name via hostel_id), it is transitive; third normal form requires splitting HOSTEL from STUDENT to remove it.

questions.question: How is a multivalued attribute such as a student's several phone numbers mapped to tables?
options: Comma-separated in one column of STUDENT
A separate table with the owner's key plus one phone per row
Extra columns phone1, phone2, phone3 in STUDENT
questions.rationale: Composite attributes flatten into plain columns, but multivalued attributes become their own table — PHONE(student_id, phone) — keeping values atomic and searchable.

questions.question: Deleting the last enrolment row for the Networks course erases the course's title and credits from the database. Which anomaly is this?
questions.rationale: A deletion anomaly is the loss of an unrelated fact because it shared a row with the deleted one — the symptom that drives decomposition into separate STUDENT, COURSE, and ENROLMENT tables.

questions.question: Which statement about keys is true?
options: Every candidate key is a superkey, but only minimal ones are candidate keys
Every superkey is a candidate key
A primary key and a foreign key are the same thing
A composite key cannot be a primary key
questions.rationale: Superkeys are any uniquely-identifying column sets; candidate keys are the minimal ones, and the primary key is whichever candidate key the designer chooses.

questions.question: The mnemonic "each attribute depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key" summarises which progression?
questions.rationale: The three clauses map onto atomic values (1NF), no partial dependencies (2NF), and no transitive dependencies (3NF) — the first three rungs of the normal-form ladder.

questions.question: For a 1:N relationship such as department to employees, where does the foreign key go?
options: A new junction table holding both keys
A foreign key added to the department table
A foreign key on the N side (employees) pointing at the 1 side (department)
Nowhere; 1:N relationships are left in the diagram
questions.rationale: The many side carries the key of the one side — each employee row stores its department's key — which permits many employees per department without redundancy.

questions.question: When is denormalisation a defensible choice?
options: When the schema fails third normal form
For measured, read-heavy reporting workloads, with the application keeping duplicated columns in step
questions.rationale: Deliberate redundancy can speed simple reads, but it reintroduces anomaly risk, so it must be justified by a measured workload and guarded by application logic that keeps copies consistent.
